texts.orig: Willmer House
texts.text: Willmer House

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Willmer House is  a  grade I listed building in Farnham, Surrey, in England. Built in 1718 for a local hop merchant the  building  later  became  a  school  and  dental  surgery. Since  1961  it  has  housed  the  Museum  of  Farnham.  The building was purchased by Waverley Borough Council from Surrey County Council in 2012. Willmer House is Baroque in style and features an elaborate red-brick façade, described by the Pevsner Architectural Guide as one of the finest  in  the  country.  Architectural  historian  Nathaniel Lloyd, in 1929, described the pilasters at either end of the façade  as  "perhaps  the  most  beautiful  example  extant  of the Doric order interpreted in brick".

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A restoration of the façade in 2017 revealed it was in need of  more  significant  repair  than  had  been  thought.  Since 2018  scaffolding  has  been  in  place  to  protect  the  public from falling masonry. The council applied for Arts Council England funding in 2022 to part-fund the repairs.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Willmer  House  is  a  Baroque-style  three-storey  building with a facade of five bays facing West Street in Farnham, Surrey. [1][2]  It is constructed of red brick with detailing in moulded bricks. At either end of the façade are Doric-style brick  pilasters. [1]   Architectural  historian  Nathaniel  Lloyd described  them  in  1929  as  "perhaps  the  most  beautiful example extant of the Doric Order interpreted in brick". [3] At the top of the first-floor level a string course is formed in moulded brick while a brick cornice runs along the top of  the  second  floor.  At  the  edge  of  the  roof  is  a  brick parapet, with piers between the bays. texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  central  bay  protrudes  towards  the  street  and  features  the  main  entrance  at  ground-floor level. [1]  The door is wood with eight panels, it is surrounded by panelled pilasters, painted white, and surmounted by an entablature featuring a central cusp. [1][2]  The door is reached by two stone steps,  though  step-free  disabled  access  is  possible  by  an  adjoining  building. [1][4]   Because  of  the historic nature of the structure it has not been considered appropriate to install a lift or stair lift to provide step-free access to the upper floors. [4]  The windows are of the sash type. The windows on the upper two storeys have bolection moulded  brick  surrounds;  those  on  the  first  floor  are capped  with  segment-shaped  moulding  and  those  on  the second storey with straight moulding. [2]  The ground-floor windows have plain surrounds. [1]

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Exploring Museums: The Home Counties , a 1990 work by Nell  Hoare  and  Geoffrey  Marsh  for  the  Great  Britain Museums  and  Galleries  Commission,  describes  Willmer House  as  "one  of  the  finest  houses  in  the  town". [5]   The interior features elaborate an Ionic pilaster and entablatured archway  in the hall.  A  second  doorway dividing  a  front  and  back  room  has  Corinthian  pilasters and carved spandrels. [2]  There is a fine oak staircase and period  wood  panelling  and  fireplaces. [1][2]   The  garden features a bust of reforming local 19th-century member of parliament William Cobbett. [6]

texts.orig: History
texts.text: History

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Willmer  House  was  built  in  1718  as  a  house  for  the  local  hop  merchant  John  Thorne,  on  land parcelled off in 1710. [7][8]  The site has earlier occupation as building work in 1992-93 revealed a late mediaeval chalk wall, probably used to retain a garden terrace, a brick-lined Tudor period well, a  rubbish pit and a 17th-century cobbled surface and associated Purbeck Marble flagstone path. Pottery from the 13th and 14th centuries was also found. [9]  By the early Victorian period the house had  become  a  private  boarding  school  for  boys. [10]   It  later  housed  a  girls  school  and  a  dental surgery. [8]

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  structure  was  first  granted  statutory  protection  as  a  listed  building  on  26  April  1950.  It  is currently grade I listed and forms a group with other listed buildings on the street. [1]  The eastern garden wall, of red brick, was separately listed, in grade II, on 29 December 1972. [11]

texts.text: 21st-century repairs

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The  structure  was  purchased  by  Waverley  Borough  Council  from  Surrey  County  Council  in 2012. [12]  The new owners began a £92,000 restoration of the façade but this was halted in 2017 when the condition was found to be much worse than thought. [7]  The council was notified that significant repair work was required in 2018 and since then scaffolding has been erected to protect the public from any falling masonry, this has partially obscured the façade. [7][12][13]

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The costs of the repairs prohibited immediate work and had the potential to threaten the future of the  museum  in  the  building. [7]   In  October  2021  Waverley  Borough  Council  indicated  that  it intended to relinquish ownership of the museum to an independent trust, as it was judged to make applying  for  grants  easier. [12]   In  September  2022  the  council  bid  for  more  than  £600,000  of funding  from  the  Arts  Council  England  to  restore  the  façade.  If  granted  this  would  still  leave  a shortfall of around £200,000, towards which local councillors started a crowdfunding campaign. [13]
